title: Freight broker follow-up: build a useful contact rhythm.
seoTitle: Freight broker follow-up: build a useful contact rhythm
searchIntent: How often should freight brokers follow up with shippers?
excerpt: Plan shipper follow-up around prior conversations, a clear next action, and a cadence you can maintain.
takeaway: Follow up with context. Prioritize people who have engaged, keep a record, and adapt the rhythm to their response.

sections.title: Start with the contacts closest to a conversation.
paragraphs: Luis begins his follow-up lesson with former customers and prospects who have already engaged. Someone who has spoken with you, replied to an email, or interacted through a professional channel gives you context for the next contact. That context is more useful than treating every name as an entirely new prospect.

The working record should tell you what happened and what to do next. A contact’s details alone do not create a follow-up process. If the person mentioned a particular need or future date, that information belongs beside the next action so your message can build on the conversation.

sections.title: Separate list management from a new-contact sequence.
paragraphs: The lesson offers two ways to organize the work. One is a simple rotating list: divide engaged contacts into two groups, call one group and email the other, then reverse the approach the next week. This creates a routine without requiring you to invent the day’s work every morning.

The other is a more concentrated sequence after a new conversation. Luis describes an immediate follow-up email, then roughly two emails and one call a week for three to four weeks. Later, he reduces the rhythm to a weekly email and a call every two weeks. These are examples from his approach, not universal instructions to contact every prospect at that frequency.

sections.title: Let the customer’s response change the plan.
paragraphs: A cadence is a starting framework. If the customer gives a specific date, reason, or preferred method of contact, use it. A prospect who says the relevant decision happens next quarter has given you different information from someone actively asking about next week’s shipment.

A firm request to stop is also information to act on. Consistency should not become a reason to disregard it. The practical purpose of a contact schedule is to sustain useful conversations, not to accumulate touches regardless of the recipient’s wishes.

sections.title: Use each channel for a reason.
paragraphs: Luis discusses phone, email, and LinkedIn. His preference is to use professional networking to establish familiarity and then move substantive conversations toward direct contact. The channels can support one another when the messages share the same context.

An email after a call can capture what was discussed and make the next step easier to find. A later call can clarify an open question. A professional message may help identify the right person. Using several channels does not mean sending an identical generic pitch through all of them.

sections.title: Make the next action visible.
paragraphs: A useful follow-up record should let you resume the conversation without reconstructing it. Keep the contact, relevant freight context, last exchange, and next action together. If responsibility moved to a different person, update that rather than continuing to chase the old route.

The rotating-list approach is useful because it makes neglected contacts visible. The more intensive sequence is useful because a recent conversation can lose momentum. Choose the structure that fits the situation and your ability to carry it out thoughtfully. A complicated plan that is never maintained provides little benefit.

sections.title: Measure continuity rather than a magic number of touches.
paragraphs: The video mentions a commonly repeated number of contacts supposedly needed before a buyer acts, but Luis does not identify its source. This article does not use that number as evidence. There is no need for a universal touch count to explain why a clear, maintained follow-up process matters.

Instead, ask whether the conversation is becoming better informed. Are you learning who controls the freight? Is the timing clearer? Has the contact asked for information or a quote? Those observations help you distinguish a developing opportunity from repetitive outreach that is not producing new understanding.
